title: The raft
hook: the Buddha: a raft is for crossing, not for carrying on your head afterward (Majjhima Nikaya 22)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prodigal son, and a father who saw him far off. Your line was he ran. Did you take a step toward someone? Day eighty-four.

Look back at this week of many houses. Mencius and the child at the well. Confucius watching the river. Satyakama's plain truth. Guru Nanak's honest bread, and his feet toward the Kaaba. A father running down a road. Chinese, Hindu, Sikh and Christian stories, each from its own home. We end the week with the Buddha, and a story about something every one of those traditions has: methods. Ways of praying, sitting, learning. Useful things. And the odd question of what to do with a useful thing once it's done its job. Today's story is the raft.
screen: `A WEEK OF MANY HOUSES.` → `EVERY PATH HAS METHODS.` → `WHEN A METHOD HAS DONE ITS JOB.`

segments.voice: It's in the Middle Length Discourses, number twenty-two. The Buddha tells his monks: imagine a man on a long journey who comes to a wide river. The near bank is dangerous and frightening. The far bank is safe. There's no ferry and no bridge. So he gathers grass and sticks and branches and leaves, ties them into a raft, and paddling with his hands and feet, he makes it across. Now he's on the safe side, and he thinks: this raft was so useful to me. I should pick it up and carry it on my head wherever I go. And the Buddha asks the monks: would that man be doing the right thing with the raft? No, they say. What he should do, the Buddha says, is pull it up on the shore, or leave it floating, and go on his way. And then he says the startling part: in the same way, the teaching itself is like a raft. It's for crossing over, not for holding onto. Think about who's saying that. The Buddha is talking about his own teaching. Buddhists have discussed for centuries exactly what letting go of it means. It doesn't mean the teaching is useless; he just spent the whole story saying how useful the raft was. It means don't cling to it, don't turn it into something to own and defend. Use it to cross. You know this from ordinary life. The training wheels. The flashcards. The alarm you needed for years and then didn't. There's no shame in how much you needed a raft. The only mistake is carrying it on your head after you've reached the shore.
screen: `A WIDE RIVER, NO BRIDGE.` · `GRASS, STICKS, HANDS AND FEET.` · `CARRY IT ON YOUR HEAD?` · `THE TEACHING IS FOR CROSSING.` · then, large: `LEAVE THE RAFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put down one method that's done its job. Settle, and breathe. Think about the habits, rules and tricks you use to get through a day. Is there one you're still carrying out of habit, after it stopped helping? A way of working that fit an old job. A rule you made in a hard season that's over now. Find one. Thank it, honestly; it got you across something. Now picture setting it down on the bank, gently, and walking on a few steps without it. The bell holds the time.
The raft. The Buddha's picture of a teaching as something for crossing over, useful, and then set down on the far shore. Today's word.
Your line: leave the raft. Today, notice one thing you do only because you've always done it, and ask whether you've already crossed. Day eighty-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the simile of the raft to explain that the teachings are tools for liberation rather than possessions to cling to or argue over.

fork.setup: you've crossed the river on a raft you built. you're safe on the far bank. what do you do with the raft?
options: carry it on your head, in gratitude
leave it on the shore and go on
burn it so no one else can use it
fork.reveal: leave it: pull it ashore or let it float, and go on. the Buddha says his own teaching is like that raft, for crossing, not for holding.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: kulla, a raft. the simile of the raft is the kullupama.

trapdoor: what you thought: once you're done with something, throw it away.
what it means: use the teaching to cross, and don't cling to it or carry it as a burden.
what a scholar hears: the raft simile sits in MN 22, the Alagaddupama Sutta, beside the simile of the water snake.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the simile of the raft)
